# E7 — power and energy per phase, six models

**Generated by `bench/make_e7_report.py` from the committed `power.csv` files.** Nothing here is typed in.

This is the quantity the processing-in-memory case actually rests on. Parts A, B and C measured where the *time* goes; this measures where the *energy* goes, and the two need not agree. Every run is a 60 s idle baseline in the same power mode followed by three back-to-back loops of 60 s each — prefix-only, action-expert-only and full inference — with all four INA3221 rails sampled from sysfs at 20 Hz and tegrastats recording alongside (protocol §4).

**`prefix` is vision AND the VLM prefix together.** The study's latency work splits those two (E4d), but the power loops do not: `prefix_once` runs `embed_prefix` followed by the container's `forward`, which is one call chain, and isolating the vision encoder would need a fourth loop feeding it inputs the prefix builds internally. So this report can say what the action expert costs against everything else, and cannot say what vision costs against the VLM. T004 specifies these three loops; a vision-only loop would be a new measurement, not a re-analysis of this one.

**On the memory rail.** `VDDQ_VDD2_1V8AO` is measured at the regulator **input** (~5.04 V) and is never rescaled to 1.8 V. It is an **upper bound** on DRAM power, not DRAM power. Both its absolute value and its above-idle delta are given.

**On summing the rails.** T005 tested the four rails for double-counting and found none — a load that raised `VDD_GPU_SOC` by 51.8 W raised `VIN_SYS_5V0` by only 8.7 W — so `module` is their sum, and `module_without_memory_rail` is the three-rail sum for anyone who wants the memory rail excluded.

**Coverage: 14 of 14 planned runs.** Complete. Present: `groot_n15/all_compile_autotune`, `groot_n15/eager_fp32`, `groot_n16/all_compile_autotune`, `groot_n16/eager_fp32`, `groot_n17/eager_fp32`, `groot_n17/vlm_compile`, `pi0/bf16_both`, `pi0/eager`, `pi05/bf16_both_graphs`, `pi05/eager`, `smolvla/eager`, `smolvla/vlm_graphs`.

## Energy per inference of the whole frame, eager against best

The `full` loop is the complete inference. This is the number a robot's battery sees, and the one to quote when comparing a model against another model or against an accelerator proposal.

| model | N | eager J | best J | eager ms | best ms | energy saved | time saved | energy ÷ time saving |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| GR00T N1.5 | 4 | 13.73 | 8.33 | 251.3 | 159.6 | 1.65× | 1.57× | 1.05 |
| GR00T N1.6 | 4 | 12.41 | 9.27 | 333.0 | 163.1 | 1.34× | 2.04× | 0.66 |
| GR00T N1.7 | 4 | 13.50 | 9.69 | 381.6 | 239.8 | 1.39× | 1.59× | 0.88 |
| π0 | 10 | 37.09 | 18.16 | 1083.2 | 424.7 | 2.04× | 2.55× | 0.80 |
| π0 | 4 | 29.75 | 15.12 | 722.6 | 323.1 | 1.97× | 2.24× | 0.88 |
| π0.5 | 10 | 132.99 | 21.85 | 3041.6 | 482.1 | 6.09× | 6.31× | 0.96 |
| SmolVLA | 10 | 14.12 | 3.77 | 740.7 | 88.2 | 3.74× | 8.40× | 0.45 |

**The last column is the one to watch.** Above 1 means the optimised configuration saves proportionally MORE energy than time — it is removing work, not just running it sooner. Below 1 means it is buying speed with power, and the latency figure overstates the benefit. Either is possible and only measurement distinguishes them; this is why E7 exists alongside Part B.

**With all 14 points measured, it goes both ways.** Six of the seven model/N combinations save proportionally LESS energy than time — SmolVLA worst at 0.45, meaning its 8.4× speedup buys only 3.7× the energy. But **GR00T N1.5 is 1.05**: it saves slightly more energy than time, so its optimisation genuinely removes work rather than running the same work sooner. Any statement of the form "optimisation always trades power for speed here" is falsified by that row, and I made it before N1.5 was measured.

**Compare like with like.** An earlier commit message of mine put π0.5's energy saving at 6.6× against a 6.2× latency saving and concluded the optimisation was removing work rather than trading power for speed. That was wrong: 6.6× was the sum of the `prefix` and `ae` loops' above-idle energy, which is not the whole frame, set against the whole frame's latency. On the `full` loop, like for like, π0.5 saves 6.09× the energy and 6.31× the time — its optimised configuration draws slightly MORE power (45.33 W against 43.72 W), so it is buying a little speed with power. The sub-phase table below is for attributing energy WITHIN a frame; this table is for comparing frames.

## Where the energy goes, against where the time goes

The share columns are of the two measured sub-phases only (`prefix` + `ae`); `full` is listed separately because it is the whole inference including the parts neither loop isolates.

The last column is the one to read: the expert's share of the ENERGY divided by its share of the TIME. Below 1 means the expert is the cheap phase — it occupies the frame without drawing the power — and a memory-side accelerator aimed at it addresses less of the joules than of the milliseconds, by exactly that factor.

**Read the last four columns against each other.** If a phase's energy share and time share are equal it draws the average power of the frame; if its energy share is higher it is the power-hungry phase, and a memory-side accelerator aimed at it saves more energy than its latency share suggests. If lower, the opposite — and the latency argument overstates the energy case.

## Why π0's ratio is so much lower, and how to check it

π0's expert is 0.32–0.40 while every other model's is 0.69–0.83. The hypothesis, from E5: **the ratio should track the phase's GPU-idle fraction.** Idle time occupies the frame and draws almost no power above idle, so a phase that is mostly idle must have an energy share well below its time share — by roughly `1 − idle_frac`.

E5 measured π0's `ae_step` at **84.3 % GPU idle**, against vision at 1.2 % and the VLM prefix at 1.6 %. π0's action expert launches ~968 kernels per denoising step with a 62 µs median gap between them: it is dispatch-bound, and a dispatch-bound phase is cheap in joules precisely because the GPU is doing nothing for most of it.

**This is a prediction, not a result.** E5's per-region idle fraction has been measured for π0 only. The E5 matrix now queued measures it for all six, and if the hypothesis is right SmolVLA's expert — ratio 0.83 — should be markedly less idle than π0's. If it is not, the hypothesis is wrong and this section should say so rather than be quietly dropped.

## What these loops are, and what they are not

**The `prefix` and `ae` loops are driven below the policy's own entry point.** `prefix` calls `embed_prefix` and the container's `forward` with `use_cache=True`; `ae` calls `denoise_step` N times on a KV cache computed once. For GR00T the equivalents are `model.backbone(...)` and `action_head.get_action(...)` on a backbone output computed once. That is the only way to isolate the action expert for a power measurement, and it has two consequences that are stated rather than buried:

* A compile **mode** is applied to `sample_actions`, which sits ABOVE these two calls, so under `--modes` they run eager whatever was requested. The `exec_style` column says which: `eager_subpath` means exactly that. The runs labelled with a ladder **rung** compile `embed_image`, `container.forward` and `denoise_step` themselves, so there the loops are genuinely compiled (`compiled_subpath`).
* `ae_once` drives a bounded Python loop instead of `sample_actions`' GPU-tensor `while` test. That is a documented protocol §2 deviation, made because isolating the expert requires it.

**The sampler is not free.** The rail thread reads four sysfs files 20 times a second inside the measured process, and π0's eager `ae_step` is 84 % GPU-idle (E5 — the frame as a whole is 55 % at N=10, and vision and the prefix are under 2 %) — dispatch-bound work is precisely what extra host activity slows. The table below puts each loop's own median next to Part B's median for the same configuration so the perturbation is visible instead of implicit.

| model | N | configuration | E7 `full` loop median ms | Part B e2e median ms | ratio |
|---|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|
| GR00T N1.5 | 4 | `all_compile_autotune` | 159.65 | 168.75 | 0.95× |
| GR00T N1.5 | 4 | `eager_fp32` | 251.27 | 255.22 | 0.98× |
| GR00T N1.6 | 4 | `all_compile_autotune` | 163.06 | 174.59 | 0.93× |
| GR00T N1.6 | 4 | `eager_fp32` | 333.00 | 327.22 | 1.02× |
| GR00T N1.7 | 4 | `eager_fp32` | 381.65 | 372.48 | 1.02× |
| GR00T N1.7 | 4 | `vlm_compile` | 239.85 | 240.49 | 1.00× |
| π0.5 | 10 | `bf16_both_graphs` | 482.09 | 487.81 | 0.99× |
| π0.5 | 10 | `eager` | 3041.59 | 3028.56 | 1.00× |
| π0 | 10 | `bf16_both` | 424.68 | 424.46 | 1.00× |
| π0 | 10 | `eager` | 1083.19 | 1069.04 | 1.01× |
| π0 | 4 | `bf16_both` | 323.11 | — | — |
| π0 | 4 | `eager` | 722.55 | 711.75 | 1.02× |
| SmolVLA | 10 | `eager` | 740.69 | 727.46 | 1.02× |
| SmolVLA | 10 | `vlm_graphs` | 88.20 | 92.30 | 0.96× |

A ratio near 1.00 means the sampler cost nothing measurable. A ratio above 1 is the cost of measuring, and the energy-per-inference figures above carry it: they are `mean power × this loop's median`, so a slowed loop inflates the joules proportionally. Where the ratio is large, treat the **power** columns as the trustworthy ones and the **energy** columns as an upper bound.
